analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies and individuals import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and other approved countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to write rules letting U.S. pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import prescription drugs from Canada, where the same medicines often cost far less. It would have covered insulin and biologic drugs, let people fill U.S. prescriptions at licensed foreign pharmacies for up to a 90-day personal supply, banned drugmakers from punishing foreign sellers who export to Americans, and imposed safety requirements like seller certification, product testing, and criminal penalties for counterfeit-drug websites. It never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay high prescription drug prices — including people who buy insulin and other biologics — would gain access to the same drugs at Canadian prices, plus new consumer protections against counterfeit online pharmacies.

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to write rules allowing pharmacies and wholesalers to import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada within 180 days of enactment, replacing the current system where importation is only allowed if HHS certifies it first — a certification no administration has ever given [S2] [S3].
Lets individuals fill U.S. prescriptions directly through certified foreign pharmacies for personal use, up to a 90-day supply, without a special HHS waiver [S2] [S3].

Extends eligibility to insulin, biologics, and other drugs excluded from current importation law, and after two years allows importation from other countries with comparable drug-safety standards [S3].

Makes it illegal for manufacturers to charge foreign sellers higher prices than domestic Canadian buyers or to cut off supply to block importation, and adds criminal penalties for websites selling counterfeit drugs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would lose the ability to charge U.S. patients and pharmacies higher prices than Canadians pay, and U.S. pharmacies and drug wholesalers would face new competition from certified foreign sellers.

drawbacks.text: Opening U.S. consumers to foreign-supplied drugs carries some safety risk, which is why current law requires HHS to certify importation is safe before allowing it; the bill removes that certification requirement and replaces it with regulatory safeguards, testing, and suspension authority [S2] [S3].

Drugmakers could still limit the supply available for export; the bill bans discriminatory pricing and supply restrictions, but enforcement against global manufacturers would be difficult, and Canada has previously objected that it cannot supply the U.S. market [S3].
Importation targets the symptom — high U.S. list prices — rather than the underlying pricing system, so savings depend entirely on foreign price differences persisting [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is lower drug prices for people who pay out of pocket, and the safety risks are addressed seriously — certified sellers, testing laboratories, recall requirements, supply-chain tracing, and criminal penalties for counterfeit online pharmacies. The real weaknesses are practical: drugmakers could still find ways to limit Canadian supply, and the volume of safe exportable drugs from Canada's smaller market may not lower U.S. prices much. But the bill died without even a committee vote, so its design was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee, which held a subcommittee hearing but never voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 23, 2021 by Sen. Sanders with 21 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents [S1] [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S1] [S5].
A HELP subcommittee held a hearing on the bill, but the full committee never marked it up and the Senate never voted on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers keep charging Americans higher prices without Canadian competition, and no one else gained.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 21 cosponsors.

for.name: 21 Senate cosponsors (20 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Manchin, giving it some cross-ideological Democratic support.

for.name: HELP Subcommittee on Primary Health and Retirement Security
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill (S.Hrg. 117-176).

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, held only a subcommittee hearing, and never reported it out for a Senate vote.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer industry (PhRMA and brand-name drug makers)
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed drug importation legislation, arguing it undermines patent pricing and drug safety.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, and no Senate Republican signed on; the bill went nowhere in a chamber split 50-50. [S4]

industries.note: The bill forces them to sell to certified Canadian exporters at Canadian prices and bans them from charging exporters more or cutting off supply to block importation, directly threatening the higher U.S. prices they currently charge [S3].
They would face new competition from certified foreign pharmacies selling directly to American patients, including online [S3].
They gain a new, regulated export market to U.S. patients and importers, with certification fees and testing requirements they must meet [S3].
